writeup.1: All-black is the easiest look in golf to describe and the hardest to assemble, because roughly half of what the industry sells as black is not black. It is charcoal, or gunmetal, or garment-washed to a soft grey, or a navy so deep it only shows itself next to the real thing. Put two of those together on a first tee and the effect collapses.
writeup.2: The colourway name is no guide to any of that. Brands sell charcoal as black and washed grey as black, and the gap stays invisible until the piece is on a body in daylight, next to something that actually is black.
writeup.3: Near-black turns up all over the category. Siegelman’s black hoodies are vintage-dyed to a visible faded grey. Devereux’s Anorak is a black and graphite colourblock. Malbon’s jackets carry blue zips or white side panels. BestGrips sells a putter cover whose file name says black and whose photograph is unmistakably green. Royal Albartross makes handsome shoes and every men’s pair has a contrast sole, welt or heel counter. Artisan’s darkest putter finish is called Gunmetal, which is at least honest.
writeup.4: What holds up is nineteen pieces, one per brand, head to toe — two trousers, three collars, two tees, a hoodie, shorts, shoes, socks, a bag, a headcover, a belt, a cap, a towel and one thousand-dollar putter. Two things the independent end of golf does not make: a black glove from anybody, and a black sock from more than one brand.
